newsitem.title: USA: Letter proves Noriega witness took bribe - lawyers.
newsitem.headline: Letter proves Noriega witness took bribe - lawyers.

text.p: Lawyers for Gen. Manuel Noriega on Thursday demanded a new trial for the former Panamanian leader, saying a cryptic letter to Cali cartel leaders proved the cartel bribed a key witness at his trial.

The lawyers also said that the letter showed the U.S. government relied on perjured testimony to turn away Noriega's previous bid for a new trial on the grounds that witness Ricardo Bilonick, former Panamanian diplomat turned drug trafficker, accepted a $1.25 million payoff to testify.
The Cali cartel was a rival of the Medellin drug cartel, also from Colombia, with which prosecutors said Noriega was linked.

Based on the letter, attorneys Frank Rubino and Jon May filed a new petition in Miami U.S. District Court on Thursday for a new trial for Noriega, convicted in 1992 on racketeering and drug charges and now serving a 40-year prison sentence.
"It's a smoking gun and this should cause the court to reconsider," May said at a Miami news conference.

Wilfredo Fernandez, a spokesman for the Miami U.S. Attorney's Office, declined to comment on specifics of the letter but said it related to matters that had already been considered by an appeals court.
"This is an act of desperation," Fernandez said of Noriega's claim for a new trial.

The 11th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Atlanta on Monday turned down a previous Noriega bid for a new trial, ruling that the conviction would not have been altered if the jury had been told a federal witness had been paid.
The government has said it had no knowledge of a bribe and Bilonick has denied that he testified in return for a payment.

Rubino said on Thursday that the June 14, 1991 letter, found by federal investigators in the Washington law office of Michael Abbell, a former Justice Department lawyer now on trial in Miami on drug charges, proved that a bribe was paid.
The cryptic missive, addressed to "Don Manuel," does not mention Bilonick or Noriega by name and is signed by Francisco Laguna, a former Abbell colleague.
The letter refers to "the man in Panama" and says "the man's apartment rent has to be paid." Rubino and May said the "man in Panama" is Bilonick and "rent" was a reference to bribe money.
Bilonick, a Noriega co-defendant turned witness who served three years in prison, testified that Noriega allowed him to take tons of cocaine to Miami from Panama in the 1980s.
Noriega was captured by U.S. military forces following the 1989 invasion of Panama and brought to Miami.
